extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, political communication researchers, and journalism professionals interested in news bias and newsworthness
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how journalists' personal political ideology influences news-selection decisions (story choice, source selection, framing) across national media systems using comparative survey/quasi-experimental methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-National Stability
rubrics_metrics.description: In all five countries, journalists' personal ideology predicted their news-decision preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ideological influence as a cross-national phenomenon when modeling news-selection; comparative analyses should expect consistent directional effects across different media systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate Effect Size
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect was moderate in magnitude, not overwhelming — consistent with journalists' self-perception that they constrain their personal views, but not consistent with claims of perfect objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model bias as measurable but limited; avoid assuming either perfect objectivity or wholesale partisanship. Quantitative analyses should report effect sizes and interpret them as moderate rather than categorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic-Variant Influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects strongest on stories with clear partisan implications; weakest on routine procedural news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect larger ideological effects on politically charged or clearly partisan topics; when coding items, distinguish topic types (partisan vs. routine) and test for interaction with ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-Variant Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Italy showed the strongest ideology-decision link; US/UK the weakest, hypothesized to reflect media-system differences (e.g., Hallin & Mancini's Liberal vs. Polarized Pluralist models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for national media-system characteristics; do not assume uniform magnitude of ideological influence across countries or systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience to Professional Norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Even journalists who endorsed strong objectivity norms showed measurable ideological influence in their decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on self-reported professional norms as indicators of unbiased practice; incorporate behavioral or choice-based measures to detect underlying bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideologically Compatible Source Preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are more likely to lead with sources whose views align with their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating source selection, measure alignment between journalist ideology and source perspective; use placement/lead metrics to detect preferential highlighting of ideologically concordant sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideologically Compatible Frame Preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Among multiple legitimate framings of an event, journalists choose framings closer to their own views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code framing options for ideological valence and test whether journalists select frames congruent with their beliefs; frame-choice analyses should be central to assessing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Selection from Among Alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple stories of equal news value compete, journalists' preferences tip toward stories that resonate ideologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize 'competing stories' scenarios in experimental or observational work to detect selection bias; compare choices when objective news value is held constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical-Tone Asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists apply more critical scrutiny to actors and policies they oppose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tone and critique asymmetry measures (e.g., sentiment, critical language frequency) and test whether negative tone is disproportionately directed at ideologically opposed actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold Asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories supportive of journalists' views may require lower magnitude/drama to become newsworthy compared with opposing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate differing thresholds for story selection by ideological congruence; consider coding story attributes (magnitude, novelty, drama) and modeling their interaction with journalist ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-conscious Selection (Filtering Mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists may not be aware of ideological tilt in their decisions; the filter operates below explicit reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use implicit measures, choice experiments, and behavioral indicators rather than relying only on self-report; account for unconscious processes in bias detection designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine Reinforcement (Filtering Mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom routines (which sources to call, which beats to staff) embed ideological assumptions over time and reinforce bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate organizational routines and practices as mechanisms sustaining bias; include longitudinal or process-focused analyses to capture reinforcement effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Selection into Outlets (Filtering Mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists self-sort into outlets matching their views, compounding outlet-level ideological coloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish individual-level ideological effects from selection effects by outlet; consider modeling selection processes or using outlet fixed effects to separate compositional from behavioral bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlet-level Ideological Coloration as Predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlet identity/ideological coloration is empirically detectable and can be used as a predictor of placement and selection decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include outlet ideology as a covariate in newsworthiness models; treat outlet identity as a meaningful predictor of placement, framing, and source-choice patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias as Structural and Predictive (Implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is neither fully objective nor fully partisan; bias is moderate, measurable, and structural, and helps predict phenomena like the rise of partisan outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model bias as a structural factor in media analyses and avoid binary categorizations; use empirical measures of ideological influence to predict outlet-level and system-level partisan phenomena.
